prompt: A hospital network's average emergency-department wait time rose to 58 minutes versus a target of 35 minutes at one flagship site. Diagnose the deviation using the operational data given.
context: Data available: ED bed occupancy averaged 96% this month (target 85%). Average length of stay for admitted patients awaiting an inpatient bed ("boarding time") rose to 4.1 hours from a typical 1.8 hours. Triage-to-first-provider-contact time was 22 minutes, roughly in line with the 20-minute target. Inpatient bed occupancy hospital-wide was 91% (target 80%), driven partly by a reported rise in flu-related admissions this month.

binaryCriteria.description: Explicitly notes that triage-to-provider-contact time (22 min) is near its 20-minute target, ruling out ED front-door speed as the driver of the overall wait-time miss.
binaryCriteria.guidance: Fail if the answer attributes the wait-time increase to slow triage/provider response without acknowledging this metric is on target.

binaryCriteria.description: Correctly identifies boarding time (patients awaiting an inpatient bed) as the primary driver, connecting it to hospital-wide inpatient occupancy at 91% vs. 80% target.
binaryCriteria.guidance: Fail if the answer does not connect ED wait time to the boarding/inpatient-capacity chain.

binaryCriteria.description: Recommends investigating inpatient discharge throughput/bed capacity as the lever, rather than ED-specific process changes (e.g., "add more triage nurses").
binaryCriteria.guidance: Fail if the recommendation focuses only on ED front-door staffing/process without addressing inpatient capacity.

goldNotes: A strong diagnostic answer connects the dots: the wait-time miss is not explained by triage/provider-contact speed (22 vs 20 min target — roughly on track), so the bottleneck is downstream — specifically ED boarding time (patients awaiting an inpatient bed) more than doubling to 4.1 hours from 1.8, itself driven by hospital-wide inpatient occupancy at 91% vs an 80% target (a capacity problem upstream of the ED, plausibly linked to the flu-admission increase mentioned). The answer should explicitly rule out triage/provider speed as the driver (since it is near target) and correctly identify the true bottleneck as inpatient bed availability / boarding, not "the ED is slow to see patients". It should recommend investigating discharge-throughput and inpatient capacity levers, not ED front-door process changes.
